synopsis: Closed-loop agreement is the ultimately relevant validation layer for automatic braking: matched real and simulated runs must agree on brake timing, stopping trajectory or location, clearance, and false or missed interventions—not merely image similarity [f14803, f14804, f14805, f4444]. Existing warning-system history can validate inputs and submodels, but replay cannot establish the consequences of a changed machine trajectory; after the first new brake command, evidence depends on the machine, environment and sensor models [f191, f1102, f14807, f14808]. Separately validated perception and brake models do not establish combined safety, because timing, communications, saturation and operator interactions can produce emergent failures; physical full-system stopping tests should therefore remain at the collision/no-collision boundary [f8196, f8197, f14812]. An on-road IDIADA–MathWorks demonstration recorded on 14 April 2026 correlated a closed-loop AEB simulation with production-vehicle proving-ground tests using ISO 18571 metrics, but no public demonstration was found jointly covering heavy machines, many geometries, more than 100 site types, severe weather and soiling, and closed-loop braking [f1269, f4409].
